newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: TENNIS-SPAIN RUNNING HOT AT AUSTRALIAN OPEN.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-SPAIN RUNNING HOT AT AUSTRALIAN OPEN.

text.p: The biggest names of Spanish tennis have melted into the background at the Australian Open, but Spain itself is still running hot.
Searing heat has taken its toll of the top seeds of the women's singles, including big-name Spaniards Conchita Martinez and Arantxa Sanchez Vicario who wilted at the weekend.

But it is a different story in the men's draw, where three dark horses of Spanish tennis have bolted into the quarter-finals, demonstrating the depth, versatility and stamina of the nation's tennis talent.
Unseeded Carlos Moya, the tournament's giant-killer after beating defending champion Boris Becker in the first round, and 14th seed Felix Mantilla led the charge.
"I think here in Australia, I'm like a cat: I have seven lives. I am still alive," Moya told reporters after winning a five-set battle with Swede Jonas Bjorkman at the weekend.
Moya draws big crowds of young female fans to his matches and must now face Mantilla in a Barcelona baseline derby on centre court on Tuesday morning.
The winner will be the first male Spaniard to appear in the semifinals at the Australian Open for 30 years.

Tenth seed Albert Costa, who also calls Barcelona home, became the third Spaniard into quarter-finals on Monday, after eighth seeded Wayne Ferreira of South Africa cleared a path for him by retiring with a leg injury.

Costa won the first two sets and was ahead 3-2 in the third when Ferreira broke down. His victory sealed Spain's best-ever grand slam performance on hardcourts and dealt another blow to the myth that Spaniards were mere clay courters.

"There's a tradition that used to be that Spanish players almost only played on clay and there was a lot of criticism about that among the Spanish players...," said Miguel Zubiarrain, editor of Spain's Grand Slam Tennis magazine.
"The players finally realised that to win the big (ranking) points in the circuit, you have to play hardcourt tournaments," Zubiarrain added.
The Spaniards have shown a friendly camaraderie so far in the tournament, but that will evaporate when Mantilla meets his old training partner and good friend Moya on Tuesday.

"We practise together and it's not easy playing against a friend. But when you are in the quarter-finals of a grand slam, we are not friends," Mantilla said after beating 1996 Wimbledon finalist MaliVai Washington in the fourth round on Sunday.
As for Costa, he has the bad luck to face world number one Pete Sampras in his quarter-final but appears undaunted.
"It's really difficult to play with him, but I'm going to try to win," he told reporters.
The breadth of Spain's success on the Rebound Ace surface of Melbourne Park has come as a surprise to many here, but will come as no shock to tennis aficionados in Spain.
Spanish ranks have thinned out with the loss of Martinez and Sanchez Vicario, but so far this Australian Open is their best overall grand slam performance on hardcourt, Zubiarrain said.
Mantilla said on Sunday that he and his compatriots had only begun training and playing seriously on hardcourts a month ago.

"I think that the mentality of the Spanish people before is a little bit 'only play on clay courts', but now is changing -- the mentality -- and now we're playing well on this surface," Mantilla told reporters.
Clay is still king in Spain, but times are changing, thanks to the overseas feats of Spain's new hardcourt Armada. But there is another reason: more hardcourts are being built in Spain.

"There's a little bit of change, especially for economical reasons because the maintenance of clay courts is much higher than the hardcourt, so the clubs now try to build as much hardcourt as possible," said Zubiarrain.
